\title{How Much Energy Does a Modal Contact Row Inject?\\
  A Cross-Formulation Measurement and a Cumulative Storage Bound}

\author{Anonymous Author(s)}

\begin{abstract}
Unilateral contact between reduced (modal) deformable bodies and rigid bodies
is commonly resolved by a velocity-level complementarity law in which one
shared multiplier couples the rigid and modal unknowns. Interactive solvers
evaluate this law under small, fixed local iteration budgets; we measure the
energetic cost of that truncation. Running one transcribed contact row through
three fixed-budget solver formulations --- position-based (XPBD),
augmented-Lagrangian (AVBD), and an implicit sequential-impulse realization ---
over an identical 24-cell scene\,$\times$\,relaxation\,$\times$\,budget sweep,
we observe sharply formulation-dependent behaviour. Measured against the gross
rigid-side loss (a scene-wide, gravity-corrected quantity, not a per-contact
dissipation), the position-based host overdraws by up to $4.4\times10^{7}$~J
--- $1.2\times10^{5}$ times the incident rigid kinetic energy in the most
starved cells --- whereas the augmented-Lagrangian host overdraws in $23$ of
$24$ cells by at most $15$~J, and the implicit realization never overdraws.
These are distinct pathologies --- one pervasive but negligible, the other rare
but catastrophic --- and the customary ratio-to-incident-energy diagnostic does
not separate them. An iteration-budget sweep identifies the position-based
amplification as a truncation artifact: it decays monotonically toward a
converged reference computed in the same code path, closing the gap by six
orders of magnitude. Since the converged regime is unaffordable at interactive
budgets, we introduce a cumulative
modal-storage bound funded by the measured gross rigid-side loss and enforced
by a reservoir ledger and a projection of the realized modal state.
The bound holds in all 90 measured cells ($78$ distinct configurations),
including the $1{\times}8$ and $2{\times}4$ budgets at which interactive
solvers are commonly deployed. Enforcement in turn costs contact validity:
worst-case post-projection penetration reaches $21.6$~mm, $72\%$ of the
supporting board's thickness.
\end{abstract}

% =====================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% =====================================================================
A deformable object that is struck at one point and rings elsewhere is
routinely modelled by projecting the elastic response onto a small modal basis.
When such a body also rests in unilateral contact with rigid bodies, the
established treatment resolves rigid and modal unknowns together through a
shared contact multiplier at the velocity level~\citep{zheng2011}. The one-way
alternative --- driving a separate modal filter from contact events without
back-reaction --- is the real-time precedent~\citep{james2002dyrt,
coevoet2020distant}. Interactive modal deformation subject to collision and
contact constraints predates both~\citep{hauser2003}.

We take this coupled row as given. Written at position level it sits one
linearization step from the velocity-level law: for a gap function $C$,
$C^{n+1}\approx C^{n}+h\,\mathbf{J}\mathbf{u}^{n+1}$, which divided by $h$
recovers the velocity-level complementarity condition with a $C^{n}/h$
stabilization bias, carrying the same Jacobian and the same multiplier
as~\citet{zheng2011}. The row itself is \emph{not} a contribution of this
paper, and our transcription is narrower than the original law: modes couple
through normal rows only, and the position-level form assumes $e=0$
restitution.

Interactive solvers, however, do not solve this row to convergence: they run a
fixed, small number of local iterations per substep, and it is known that
finite-iteration coupling across a partition boundary can inject spurious
energy even when every subsystem is individually
passive~\citep{wei2026earlyterm} --- an observation that likewise predates this
work. Velocity-level frictional contact spanning rigid and reduced deformable
bodies, with the energy artifacts of iterative solvers named, goes back at
least to~\citet{kaufman2008}. What is missing is a quantitative account of this
case --- unilateral contact-to-modal transfer --- and a mitigation that fits
within an interactive budget.

\paragraph*{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Measurement.} A single contact row evaluated in three
  fixed-budget solver formulations over one identical 24-cell adversarial
  sweep on one machine (\S\ref{sec:matrix}), plus an iteration-budget sweep
  against a converged reference identifying the position-based injection as a
  truncation artifact (\S\ref{sec:kconv}).
\item \textbf{A cumulative storage bound.} A one-directional bound on the
  energy entering modal storage, funded by the measured gross rigid-side loss
  and enforced by a reservoir ledger and a projection of the realized modal
  state (\S\ref{sec:bound}); it satisfies the prescribed inequality in all
  $90$ measured cells ($78$ distinct configurations).
\item \textbf{The cost of enforcement.} Post-projection contact validity
  (penetration, corrective impulse, multiplier variance, momentum), measured
  rather than assumed (\S\ref{sec:validity}).
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph*{Relation to concurrent energy-control work.}
\citet{wei2026earlyterm} guarantee discrete passivity for any finite
inner-iteration budget via Douglas--Rachford splitting in wave
coordinates whose Fej\'{e}r monotonicity supplies algorithmic dissipation; their
interfaces are \emph{bilateral} couplings, not unilateral contact, and the
guarantee is structural rather than a budgeted transfer cap.
\citet{you2026energy} modify implicit Euler to track user-specified
\emph{total}-energy targets bidirectionally on full nonlinear elastodynamics
with barrier contact. Ours is neither: a one-directional cap on what contact
may deposit into modal storage, funded by measured gross rigid-side loss and
enforced by scaling realized modal state. For flexible bodies in a game engine,
\citet{zobel2025unity} solve ray-traced penalty contact quasi-statically without
a shared unilateral multiplier; modes and modal derivatives have been used in a
position-based host as a \emph{deformation} surrogate~\citep{peng2024reduced},
whereas here modal amplitudes enter as contact DOFs driven by the shared
multiplier.

\paragraph*{Relation to passivity control and energy projection.} The governor
transplants an established control idea rather than inventing one. Time-domain
passivity control~\citep{hannaford2002} damps once an energy observer goes
negative; energy-tank formulations~\citep{franken2011} give that observer
explicit state, so a controller spends only what its tank holds;
\citet{rath2008} enforces exact per-interface energy stability for contacting
modal objects at audio rate, where we cap a scene-level scalar reservoir. We
keep that structure and change two things: the tank is funded by
\emph{measured gross rigid-side loss} --- energy the solve removed elsewhere
--- rather than by the port it regulates, and the actuator scales realized
\emph{state} rather than modulating a force, because a fixed-budget solver
commits its multipliers before the excess is observable.
FEPR~\citep{dinev2018fepr} also projects state post-solve, but onto
conservation of \emph{total} energy; ours is one-sided and never restores
energy the solver lost.

% =====================================================================
\section{The row and the cumulative bound}
\label{sec:bound}
% =====================================================================
Let $\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}$ be mass-normalized modal amplitudes of the
supporting body, so its modal mechanical energy is
$\Emod=\tfrac12\dot{\mathbf{q}}^{\!\top}\dot{\mathbf{q}}
      +\tfrac12\mathbf{q}^{\!\top}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{q}$.
A support-contact row between a rigid corner at world height $y_c$ and the
deformed surface has gap
\begin{equation}
C \;=\; y_c \;-\; \bigl(y_{\mathrm{rest}} + \mathbf{U}_y^{\!\top}\mathbf{q}\bigr),
\qquad C \ge 0,\; \lambda \ge 0,\; C\lambda = 0,
\label{eq:row}
\end{equation}
with $\partial C/\partial\mathbf{q}=-\mathbf{U}_y$, so one multiplier $\lambda$
drives both the rigid body and the modal amplitudes. Equation~\eqref{eq:row} is
the transcription discussed above, not a new law.

\paragraph*{The invariant.} We require that the energy \emph{stored in the
modal subsystem} never exceed the \emph{measured gross rigid-side loss} ---
defined exactly at \eqref{eq:derig} below --- cumulatively over the run:
\begin{equation}
\Emod^{\,n} - \Emod^{\,0}
\;\;\le\;\;
\eta \sum_{k\le n} \max\!\bigl(\dErig^{\,k},\,0\bigr),
\qquad \eta\in(0,1].
\label{eq:invariant}
\end{equation}
The transfer efficiency $\eta$ sets how much of the measured loss may be spent;
\emph{every experiment in this paper runs $\eta=1$}, the least restrictive
admissible value, so no result below depends on tuning it. The bound is
\emph{cumulative}, not per-step: a substep may deposit more than it earns
provided the running total remains within the budget, which is what lets a
legitimate ring persist across substeps.

\paragraph*{Definitions.} Modal storage is the mechanical energy of the
reduced state as written above, and $\Emod^{\,0}=0$: every scene starts from an
undeformed, resting support, so even the run's own settling transient must be
funded by the reservoir. The supply is
\begin{equation}
\dErig^{\,k} \;=\; \bigl(E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{k,-} - E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{k,+}\bigr)
                 \;+\; W_g^{\,k},
\qquad
W_g^{\,k}=\sum_b m_b\,\mathbf{g}\!\cdot\!\bigl(\mathbf{x}_b^{k,+}-\mathbf{x}_b^{k,-}\bigr),
\label{eq:derig}
\end{equation}
where $E_{\mathrm{rig}}=\sum_b\bigl[\tfrac12 m_b\|\mathbf{v}_b\|^2
+\tfrac12\boldsymbol{\omega}_b^{\!\top}\mathbf{I}_b\boldsymbol{\omega}_b\bigr]$
is \emph{purely kinetic} --- translational and rotational, over all dynamic
bodies, not merely those in contact --- and $\pm$ denote the two ends of substep
$k$. We call this the \textbf{measured gross rigid-side loss}: the scene-wide,
gravity-corrected, gross kinetic-energy loss of the rigid subsystem. It is a
\emph{loss}, not a dissipation --- it also counts legitimate rigid-to-modal
transfer and losses at rigid--rigid contacts elsewhere in the scene --- so it is
an envelope on what contact dissipated, not a measurement of it
(\S\ref{sec:limits}). Gravity enters only through the work term $W_g$, so free
ballistic motion registers zero supply: a falling body's kinetic gain exactly
equals the gravity work, and only an inelastic velocity change funds the
reservoir. Substep-boundary endpoints tile the timeline exactly, so no rigid
energy change escapes the accounting.

\paragraph*{What is guaranteed, and what is not.} Equation~\eqref{eq:invariant}
is a \emph{cumulative, gross-loss-funded storage ceiling on the modal
subsystem}, with a supply that is \emph{measured, not prescribed}: the
right-hand side is the measured loss of \eqref{eq:derig}, never a tuned
constant or a fraction of incident energy. It is not contact-port passivity and
not a signed per-interface transfer bound --- it constrains a scalar reservoir,
not a port. The \emph{gross} sum ignores substeps in which the rigid subsystem
\emph{gains} energy, so those cannot cancel earlier credits, and energy
returned and re-dissipated counts as fresh supply; \S\ref{sec:limits} measures
both.


\paragraph*{The enforced inequality is slightly weaker than the stated one.}
Reported violations use \eqref{eq:invariant} exactly as printed. The
implementation's own test additionally forgives one substep's largest deposit,
$\max_k \eta\max(\dErig^{\,k},0)$, absorbing a granularity artifact of the
loop below: modal potential energy can rise in the very substep whose credit
funds it. That allowance is worth $7$--$389$~J here --- immaterial where the
overdraw is $10^{5}$~J or more, decisive where it is not: under it the
augmented-Lagrangian host would violate $1$ of $24$ cells rather than $23$. We
report the stricter reading throughout, for governed and ungoverned alike; the
governed runs satisfy it with a worst margin of $1.1\times10^{-13}$~J.

\paragraph*{Enforcement.} A reservoir $B$ accumulates the supply and is debited
by realized storage. Both happen \emph{after} the contact solve, within the
same substep: $\dErig$ is not observable until the velocity solve
has finalized the rigid velocities, so the substep credits
$B \leftarrow B + \eta\max(\dErig,0)$ at that point, tests the realized modal
energy against it, and only then debits
$B \leftarrow \max(B - \max(\Delta\Emod,0),\,0)$. If
the realized modal energy would overdraw $B$, the state is projected onto the
admissible set by a single scalar,
\begin{equation}
(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) \;\leftarrow\; \gamma\,(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}),
\qquad
\gamma \;=\; \min\!\left(1,\;
  \sqrt{\frac{\Emod^{-} + B}{\Emod^{+}}}\right),
\label{eq:gamma}
\end{equation}
with $\Emod^{\mp}$ the modal energy before and after the solve. One substep of
the governed loop, identical in all three hosts, then reads:
\begin{enumerate}\setlength{\itemsep}{0pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}%
\setlength{\topsep}{2pt}\footnotesize
\item snapshot $E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{-}$ (pure KE, all bodies), $\Emod^{-}$, $\mathbf{x}^{-}$;
\item predict (gravity); generate contacts at the predicted pose;
\item position solve ($K$ iterations), then velocity solve --- \emph{the contact solve};
\item $\dErig=(E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{-}\!-\!E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{+})+W_g$, i.e.\ \eqref{eq:derig}, post-solve;
\item credit $B \leftarrow B + \eta\max(\dErig,0)$ --- same substep;
\item if $\Emod^{+} > \Emod^{-} + B$, scale the state by $\gamma$ of \eqref{eq:gamma};
\item debit $B \leftarrow \max(B-\max(\Delta\Emod,0),\,0)$. Contact is \textbf{not} re-solved.
\end{enumerate}
The form \eqref{eq:gamma} is closed because $\Emod$ is quadratic in the state:
scaling $\mathbf{q}$ and $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$ together scales both the kinetic
and the elastic term by $\gamma^2$, so $\gamma$ bounds the total energy rather
than the velocity alone. Two consequences are measured below: the projection
is inert whenever the solve is within budget ($\gamma=1$, bitwise-identical
trajectories), and it never re-solves contact (step~7).

% =====================================================================
\section{Results}
% =====================================================================
All solver-behaviour measurements below come from a single machine
(Table~\ref{tab:solvers}), the sole exception being the device-resident timings
of \S\ref{sec:cost} (NVIDIA RTX 4090), reported separately; every number is
frozen with its generating command and commit hash in the supplemental ledger.
We deliberately avoid mixing machines: chaotic contact stacks diverge across
architectures under floating-point reassociation.

\subsection{One row, three formulations, the same 24 cells}
\label{sec:matrix}

peak modal energy / peak incident rigid kinetic energy, log scale diverging at

$2/24$, the implicit realization in $0/24$. \textbf{Bottom:} the invariant

We drive an impactor into a modally reduced support in three scenes --- a shelf
board, a ledge slab, and a $2.2\times1.1$~m table, the last two following the
layouts of \citet{coevoet2020distant} --- and sweep modal relaxation and the
local budget (iterations $\times$ substeps) over
$\{4{\times}1, 8{\times}2, 16{\times}4, 32{\times}8\}$.
Table~\ref{tab:solvers} lists what the hosts do differently and what is pinned
identical. Two entries deserve emphasis. The relaxation axis is \emph{inert} on
the impulse host: its implicit modal weight needs no under-relaxation and the
attribute is never read (hence the bit-identical hatched rows of
Fig.~\ref{fig:matrix}). Warm-start policy also differs. We run
each host as published: $\lambda\!\leftarrow\!0$ every substep is the
position-based host's own form, and carried duals with a growing penalty are
constitutive of the augmented-Lagrangian method, so neither is our choice; the
impulse host's per-row $\lambda$ cache is the only genuine policy default among
the three. The comparison is therefore as-deployed, not compliance-matched.

\paragraph*{Equal row evaluations, unequal outcome.} A cell costs $K\!\cdot\!S$
row evaluations per frame, so the budget axis spans $\times64$ and conflates
two refinements that are neither interchangeable nor equally priced --- a
substep also repeats contact generation and integration, so equal-sweep cells
are not equal-cost. With a fixed budget of $32$ row evaluations on the shelf
drop, spent as iterations ($K{=}32$, $S{=}1$) the ratio is $0.300$ and
\eqref{eq:invariant} holds; spent as substeps ($K{=}4$, $S{=}8$) it is $3.13$,
overdrawing by $481$~J: substep refinement alone does not converge the row (the
full ladder is in the supplement).

Figure~\ref{fig:matrix} shows the outcome. The position-based host exceeds
$R=1$ in $8$ of $24$ cells, worst case $1.19534\times10^{5}$ (ledge, relaxation $1.0$,
$4{\times}1$: peak modal energy $4.44\times10^{7}$~J against an incident
$371$~J). The augmented-Lagrangian host exceeds $R=1$ in $2$ of $24$ --- both at
the starved $4{\times}1$ corner of the table scene, worst $1.70$ --- so it is
not unconditionally benign either. The ordering is scene-dependent, and it
inverts: taking the worst over scenes at $4{\times}1$, the position-based host
is five orders of magnitude more energetic ($1.2\times10^{5}$ vs $1.70$), yet
on the table scene itself the augmented-Lagrangian host is the worse ($1.18$
and $1.70$ against a position-based worst of $0.37$). Neither host dominates
across scenes.

\paragraph*{The ratio is not the invariant.} An impactor's incident kinetic
energy is not the supply \eqref{eq:invariant} budgets against, so we measure
\eqref{eq:invariant} directly on all three hosts, ungoverned, running the
reservoir accounting live while forcing $\gamma\equiv1$: every state write in
the enforcement path is guarded by $\gamma<1$, so the trajectory is
bit-identical to an ungoverned run (the ratios above reproduce the independent
sweep exactly). We report the signed margin of \eqref{eq:invariant} in joules;
positive values violate. The two metrics agree on the position-based host
($8/24$ either way) and on the implicit one ($0/24$, margin at worst
$-5.7\times10^{-4}$~J), but they disagree on the augmented-Lagrangian host,
which violates \eqref{eq:invariant} in $23$ of $24$ cells although $R$ flags
only $2$. The magnitudes separate the two failures: in $21$ of its $23$ cells
the augmented-Lagrangian overdraw is below $0.15$~J (worst $15.1$~J), against
the position-based host's $4.4\times10^{7}$~J. A pervasive but negligible
overdraw and a rare but catastrophic one are different pathologies, and only
the invariant distinguishes them.

With enforcement enabled, all $72$ cells \emph{of this sweep} satisfy
\eqref{eq:invariant} --- $60$ of them distinct configurations, the implicit
host's $12$ relaxation pairs being bit-identical (Fig.~\ref{fig:matrix}); the
$18$ deployed-budget cells of \S\ref{sec:kconv} satisfy it too. The worst
realized ratio falls to $1.22$ (XPBD) and $0.87$ (AVBD), and the projection
never activates in any impulse cell, nor at the well-resolved budgets
($16{\times}4$, $32{\times}8$) on the position-based host at relaxation $0.7$:
it is inert precisely where the solve is already within budget.


\subsection{The position-based amplification is a truncation artifact}
\label{sec:kconv}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_s2_kconvergence.pdf}
\caption{Energy ratio versus local iteration budget $K$ on a deterministic
shelf drop, substeps pinned at $1$ so $K$ is the only variable, governor OFF.
The position-based host decays monotonically toward the converged reference,
crossing the incident-energy threshold between $K{=}16$ and
$K{=}24$; the gap shrinks by six orders of magnitude. The
reference is the implicit realization at $K{=}500$ --- the same code path run
to convergence, not a different model; it is already converged at $K{=}2$. The
AVBD curve is shown for completeness only: its denominator is itself
budget-dependent at small $K$, so it cannot be read as a convergence trend.}
\label{fig:kconv}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:kconv} isolates the local iteration budget. The position-based
host falls monotonically from $2.96\times10^{4}$ at $K{=}1$ to $0.300$ at
$K{=}32$, approaching the converged reference $0.2735$; the gap
$|\text{XPBD}-\text{reference}|$ shrinks from $2.96\times10^{4}$ to
$2.7\times10^{-2}$. The implicit realization moves only in the fourth decimal
across $K=2\ldots500$ (spread $4.9\times10^{-4}$).

A falling energy ratio does not by itself show that the \emph{row} is
converging --- a single scalar could shrink coincidentally. Measuring the
constraint directly resolves the question: the end-of-substep complementarity
residual $\|\min(C,\lambda)\|_\infty$ on the same sweep falls monotonically
from $2.79\times10^{-2}$ at $K{=}1$ to $3.56\times10^{-6}$ by $K{=}64$, where
it saturates ($K{=}128$ moves it only in the seventh significant figure). The
energy crossing at $K\approx24$ coincides with the residual passing
${\sim}3\times 10^{-5}$; the amplification disappears precisely as the
complementarity conditions begin to hold. We report this for the position-based host only: the
augmented-Lagrangian multiplier is not the same object, and the implicit
realization is already converged at $K{=}2$, so neither yields a comparable
curve.

\paragraph*{Self-convergence stops short of the reference.} Running the
position-based host to $K\!=\!500$ against itself does not close the remaining
gap: its ratio plateaus by $K\approx64$ ($0.3003$, $0.2999$, $0.2997$,
$0.2996$, $0.2996$ at $K=32\ldots500$), so the residual $2.6\times10^{-2}$
against the reference's $0.2735$ is a fixed point, not a tail. The state
agrees no better: on the deflection trajectory
$d_i(t)=\mathbf{U}_y[i]^{\!\top}\mathbf{q}(t)$ the peak matches to $2.4\%$ but
the trajectories differ by $\|d^{500}-d^{\text{ref}}\|_\infty = 6.8$~mm, $34\%$
of the reference's own peak, likewise flat from $K{=}32$. The two hosts
converge to different discrete solutions --- expected, since they discretize
the same continuous law differently --- so the sweep separates two easily
conflated effects: a truncation pathology that convergence removes,
superimposed on a formulation difference that it does not. (No ring frequency
is reported here: quasi-static sag dominates these windows, so the dominant
spectral peak moves with window length; \S\ref{sec:gt} has the resolved
comparison.)

This central diagnostic cuts in two directions: the amplification is created
by truncation and largely cured by convergence, so iterating further --- or
adopting the implicit formulation --- would remove the pathology outright. The
bound of \S\ref{sec:bound} is therefore not a substitute for convergence; it
targets the regime where neither escape is available. Following the
one-iteration small-step regime~\citep{macklin2019small}, interactive
position-based solvers run schedules near $1{\times}8$ to $2{\times}4$, well
below the $K\!\ge\!24$ this scene needs; these are representative stress
budgets, not universal engine defaults. Measured on $18$ further cells (3
scenes $\times$ 3 hosts $\times$ $\{1{\times}8, 2{\times}4\}$, relaxation
$0.7$), the position-based host violates \eqref{eq:invariant} in all six of its
deployed cells, worst $R=2282$ --- on $8$ row evaluations, twice the $4$ of the
$4{\times}1$ corner. The other hosts behave as in the sweep ($5/6$ and $0/6$
cells, the former by at most $0.16$~J). Governed, all $18$ satisfy
\eqref{eq:invariant} (worst $R = 1.022$), and the projection is gentler than at
$4{\times}1$: worst penetration $9.8$~mm against $21.6$.

\subsection{The cost of enforcement}
\label{sec:validity}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\footnotesize

substep. Gap violation is measured immediately after the $\gamma$-scale; the
corrective impulse is the next substep's normal impulse against the unclamped
steady-state median, a ratio because the hosts' multipliers are different
objects. The $4{\times}1$ position-based cells clamp on nearly every substep,
so no steady state exists there (---). The augmented-Lagrangian rows are its
only two cells with $R>1$.}
\label{tab:validity}
\begin{tabular}{llrrrr}
\toprule
scene & budget & clamped & gap viol.\ med / max [mm] & impulse & $\lambda$ var. \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{@{}l}{\emph{position-based}, relaxation $0.7$}\\
shelf & $4{\times}1$ & 107/108 & 1.25 / \textbf{21.6} & ---          & --- \\
shelf & $8{\times}2$ & 162/216 & 0.30 / 6.46          & $6.90\times$ & $26\times$ \\

\paragraph*{Accuracy.} Bounding the energy is useful only if the bounded
solution improves on the unbounded one. At a moderate injecting cell (shelf,
$8{\times}2$, relaxation $0.7$), peak modal energy is $1555.6$~J ungoverned and
$29.26$~J governed against the converged reference's $7.92$~J: the energy error
falls $196{\times}\to3.7{\times}$, or $+1548\to+21$~J; against the host's own
fixed point ($8.22$~J), $189{\times}\to3.6{\times}$, so the result does not
depend on the reference chosen. The trajectory, however, degrades:
$\|d-d^{\text{ref}}\|_\infty$ is $6.5$~mm ungoverned and $14.3$~mm governed,
$33\%$ and $71\%$ of the reference's peak --- the governor acts as a safety
envelope, not an accuracy device. At the deployed $1{\times}8$ cell the same
comparison gives $2823{\times}\to3.7{\times}$ on energy and the trajectory
improves as well ($108\to96\%$ of reference peak). The trade is
budget-dependent, but $96\%$ of the reference peak is still far from faithful.

This also explains how a $196\times$ energy error can coexist with a peak
deflection only $1.2\times$ too large. The excess is neither kinetic ($0.3\%$)
nor low-frequency: this scene's spectrum is bimodal (ten bending modes below
$2.1$~kHz, six stiff ones above $20$~kHz), and $99.6\%$ of the ungoverned
energy sits in the stiff cluster, ${\sim}200\times$ above the $240$~Hz substep
rate, against $0.0\%$ for both references. Being a single scalar, $\gamma$
cannot redistribute energy across the spectrum: it corrects the \emph{amount}
($1555.6\to29.3$~J), leaves the character intact ($99.6\to97.7\%$), and scales
the legitimate sag down with the noise ($24.1\to5.9$~mm against $20.0$).

\paragraph*{Contact validity.}
Since $\gamma<1$ shrinks the sag $\mathbf{U}_y^{\!\top}\mathbf{q}$,
\eqref{eq:gamma} lifts the support \emph{into} the resting body without
re-solving contact. Table~\ref{tab:validity} quantifies the consequence,
instrumented by wrappers that leave the solve unperturbed (clamp counts
reproduce the independent sweep exactly).

Median post-projection penetration is $0.07$--$1.25$~mm, but the worst case
reaches $21.6$~mm, a $3.5$--$12.6\times$ increase over its pre-scale value. The
shelf board is $30$~mm thick, so that is $72\%$ of its thickness; against the
unclamped scene at a converged budget (resting sag $1.7$--$2.4$~mm, peak
dynamic deflection $20.0$--$20.5$~mm) it is $9$--$13\times$ the sag and
$1.05$--$1.08\times$ the board's peak deflection --- a visible
interpenetration, not a sub-millimetre artifact, occurring where the projection
is most load-bearing. Contact recovers in the next substep rather
than accumulating, but that correction costs a normal impulse of up to
$8.7\times$ the steady-state value, with multiplier variance up to $58\times$
higher. Net rigid linear momentum is unchanged across the projection --- with
exactly zero drift --- in every clamp-active substep of every cell, necessarily
so since \eqref{eq:gamma} writes only modal state; we verified this numerically
rather than asserting it.

The same instrumentation on the augmented-Lagrangian host, at its only two cells
with $R>1$, finds the projection an order of magnitude gentler: a quarter of
substeps rather than nearly all, $\gamma$ no lower than $0.60$, worst-case
violations of $1.4$ and $3.1$~mm against $21.6$, and corrective impulse and
multiplier variance within $1.4\times$ of steady state where the position-based
host reaches $8.7\times$ and $58\times$. This is consistent with
\S\ref{sec:matrix} --- its overdrafts are at most $15$~J --- while the
\emph{relative} effect is comparable ($3.1$ and $5.5\times$ against
$3.5$--$12.6\times$). The hosts differ in the scale of the correction rather
than in its character.

\subsection{The reduced response against a full-FEM reference}
\label{sec:gt}
Bounding the energy is likewise useful only if the bounded response is the
correct one. On the ledge scene we compare the reduced arm against an unreduced
FEM solve of the same mesh, both built on the \emph{same} discrete operator
(the
reduced basis is $\mathrm{eigsh}(\mathbf{K},\mathbf{M})$ of the operator the
reference integrates), so discretization bias cancels from every ratio. The
reduced-to-reference peak-deflection ratio rises monotonically
$0.38\to0.54\to0.79\to0.88$ as $h$ refines $1/120\to1/960$, plateauing near
$0.9$; the residual ${\sim}10\%$ is $k{=}24$ mode truncation on a thick,
high-frequency slab, not a coupling error --- the ring frequency already agrees
to $0.4\%$ ($78.0$ vs $78.3$~Hz). The far-field shape agrees too: peak
deflection sits at the pedestal antinode rather than under the impact, and the
falloff tracks the reference at Spearman $\rho=0.89$ with no fitted attenuation
term. This is the pre-topple, small-displacement regime; we claim nothing
beyond it.

\subsection{Runtime cost}
\label{sec:cost}
On the CPU host at $16{\times}4$, over ten repetitions of $100$ frames, the
baseline step costs $11.0$--$125.6$~ms by scene and formulation, and the ledger
adds $0.23$--$0.41$~ms --- $0.9$--$3.4\%$ --- on the four shelf and ledge
configurations, where it resolves above run-to-run variance. On the table scene
it does not: the overhead's per-repetition spread exceeds its mean in both
hosts ($+1.35\pm2.08$ and $+0.04\pm1.43$~ms), so we report it only as bounded
by ${\sim}1.4$~ms. The percentage is the portable quantity: on a second machine
absolute times differ by $3.5$--$4.6\times$ while the percentages agree to
within $0.02$ points wherever both resolve. These baselines fall
$1.3$--$15\times$ short of a $120$~Hz budget, though shelf and ledge meet it at
$2{\times}4$ with the governor on.

A separate device-resident path (NVIDIA RTX 4090), which carries the
ledger read-only as a monitor rather than enforcing it, reaches
$5.0$--$8.9$~ms/step at $16{\times}4$ across four scenes (the two above, a
$2.5\times1.5$~m road slab under a dropped crate, and the table). The
shelf and ledge scenes meet a $120$~Hz budget there with margin
($1.7\times$ and $1.3\times$); the road scene sits at the boundary
($1.01\times$ on the mean, with a $9.3$~ms worst step); the table scene does
not ($0.94\times$). All four meet it at $16{\times}2$ or below. We make no
unqualified real-time claim. A device-resident \emph{enforced} $\gamma$ does
not exist in this work, so governed device timings lie outside our
measurements rather than being withheld (\S\ref{sec:limits}).

% =====================================================================
\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}
% =====================================================================
\textbf{Stability is not accuracy.} Where the projection is load-bearing it
opens contact violations up to $21.6$~mm and moves the trajectory \emph{away}
from the converged reference even as it moves the energy toward it
(\S\ref{sec:validity}). The result is bounded, not faithful; the honest use of
the bound is as a safety envelope for budgets that would otherwise diverge. A
natural next mechanism scales deviations about the quasi-static equilibrium
rather than the whole state, preserving the load-bearing sag; we have not built
it, and its unscaled equilibrium term would leave \eqref{eq:invariant} holding
only while the reservoir exceeds the sag's strain energy.

\textbf{Convergence remains the better remedy where affordable}
(\S\ref{sec:kconv}).

\textbf{Scope of the row.} The coupling is normal-only --- friction remains
body-local, so scraping and rolling transfer lie outside it --- and the
position-level form fixes $e=0$.

\textbf{The bound governs modal storage only}, not energy created spuriously in
rigid degrees of freedom --- in the impulse realization, box--box rows
rectifying a support ring into net rigid motion. The ledger is blind to this by
design.

\textbf{The supply is a gross sum, so it can be recycled.} Because the
reservoir is funded by $\sum_k\max(\dErig^{\,k},0)$, energy returning from the
modes to the rigid bodies and dissipated there is credited twice. We bound the
exposure by accumulating the opposite channel, $\sum_k\max(-\dErig^{\,k},0)$, as
a fraction of the supply: $0.4$--$27\%$ (implicit) and $3$--$32\%$
(position-based) --- larger than the ${\lesssim}1\%$ we expected, so the caveat
rests on measurement. On the augmented-Lagrangian host it reaches
$102$--$118\%$: the rigid subsystem's gross \emph{gain} exceeds its gross loss
in every cell --- the box--box rectification above, not a property of the
bound. There the supply is an upper envelope on genuinely dissipated energy;
tightening it would need the signed or per-interface accounting this scalar
reservoir deliberately avoids.

\textbf{Enforcement is host-side} and single-machine (CPU float64); a
device-resident governor and a validation of the \emph{governed} path against
a full-FEM reference remain future work.

\textbf{Formulation coverage.} Three formulations, three scenes, one contact
regime; the augmented-Lagrangian host's small but near-universal overdraft
makes any claim that descent-class solvers are passive in this setting an
empirical statement about this sweep, not a theorem.

% =====================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
% =====================================================================
Transcribing an established rigid--modal contact law into fixed-budget solvers
is not energy-safe, and how unsafe depends strongly on the formulation:
worst-case modal-to-incident ratios are $1.2\times10^{5}$, $1.70$ and $0.53$
across three hosts on the same 24 cells. The position-based amplification is a
truncation artifact convergence removes; the augmented-Lagrangian overdraft we
measure but do not explain. Where convergence is unaffordable, a cumulative
storage bound funded by measured gross rigid-side loss holds in every measured
cell, at a quantified cost to contact accuracy.
